content.text: {"primary_meaning":"A title or symbolic portrayal of the eternal God—most commonly identified in Christian interpretation as God the Father—seated as the sovereign heavenly king and judge. His great age signifies eternity, primordial authority, wisdom, and unchallengeable dominion rather than physical frailty.","primary_basis":["Daniel 7:9–10: the Ancient of Days takes his throne amid fiery judgment, with white clothing and hair and the heavenly court assembled.","Daniel 7:13–14: one like a son of man comes before the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion, supporting the customary Christian distinction between the Ancient of Days and Christ, the Son of Man.","Daniel 7:21–22: the Ancient of Days comes, renders judgment, and vindicates the saints.","Psalm 90:2 and Isaiah 40:28 are often cited as broader support for God's eternity.","Revelation 1:12–18, especially 1:14, applies imagery resembling Daniel's Ancient of Days to the risen Christ, contributing to Christological interpretations."] ,"alternatives":[{"meaning":"The Ancient of Days is Christ himself, portrayed in his eternal divine nature and as final judge.","basis":["Revelation 1:14 gives the glorified Christ white hair resembling the figure in Daniel 7:9.","Christ exercises divine judgment and possesses everlasting dominion in passages such as John 5:22–27 and Revelation 19–20.","This identification appears in portions of patristic interpretation and especially in Eastern Christian iconographic and liturgical traditions."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"The title refers simply to God as the eternal divine ruler, without assigning the figure specifically to the Father or another Trinitarian person.","basis":["Daniel 7 itself calls the figure the Ancient of Days but does not employ later Christian Trinitarian terminology.","The imagery primarily communicates divine eternity, kingship, and judicial authority."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The figure is a literary or apocalyptic personification of God's eternal kingship and heavenly court rather than a description intended to identify a distinct divine person.","basis":["Daniel 7 uses symbolic throne-room imagery, including beasts, fire, books, and a heavenly tribunal.","Historical-critical interpretation often emphasizes the vision's apocalyptic symbolism and its message of divine judgment over oppressive kingdoms."],"prominence":"minority"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad consensus that the Ancient of Days symbolizes the eternal, sovereign God acting as judge. The narrower identification with God the Father is the dominant traditional Christian reading because the Son of Man approaches him in Daniel 7:13, but it is not completely settled: some traditions identify the Ancient of Days with Christ, while others avoid specifying a Trinitarian person."}
